title: Genesis 15. The Cup Cut.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 15. The Cup Cut.
After these things,
the word of the Lord comes to Abram in a vision:
Do not be afraid, Abram.
I am your shield.
Your reward shall be very great.
Abram answers.
For the first time since God spoke in chapter twelve,
Abram speaks back.
And what he says is not worship.
It is not gratitude.
It is grief.
Lord God, what will You give me?
I continue childless.
The heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus.
You have given me no offspring.
A servant born in my house will inherit everything.
The Cup that was filled with promise, a great nation,
offspring like the dust, the land,
has arrived at a man who has no son.
The vessel that was told to count the stars in chapter thirteen still has no child.
The promise and the reality do not match.
Abram says so.
God answers: This man shall not be your heir.
One who will come from your own body shall be your heir.
Then He brings him outside.
Look toward heaven.
Count the stars, if you are able to count them.
So shall your offspring be.
Where Lot lifted up his eyes and saw a plain that would burn,
Abram is told to lift up his eyes and see stars that cannot be counted.
Where the dust of chapter thirteen measured multitude,
the stars of chapter fifteen measure impossibility.
Dust can be counted by a patient man.
Stars cannot.
The Cup that was promised to a barren woman is now measured by what cannot be numbered.
And Abram believed the Lord.
And He counted it to him as righteousness.
The first time faith is named as righteousness in Scripture.
Not what Abram did.
Not what he built.
Not what he offered.
What he believed.
The Cup is not filled by works.
It is received by faith.
The man who fumbled in Egypt, who gave away his wife,
who refused Sodom's wealth,
is called righteous because he believed God's word about a son he could not see and a wife who could not bear.
Then God speaks again:
I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans,
to give you this land to inherit.
And Abram asks: Lord God,
how will I know that I shall inherit it?
The question is not doubt.
It is the question of a man who has believed a promise and now asks for a sign.
God does not rebuke him.
He gives him an instruction.
Bring Me a heifer three years old,
a female goat three years old, a ram three years old,
a turtledove, and a young pigeon.
Abram brings them all.
He cuts the heifer, the goat, and the ram in half.
He lays each half opposite the other.
He does not cut the birds.
He arranges a corridor of death, animals divided, blood on the ground,
halves facing each other across a path that has not yet been walked.
Birds of prey come down on the carcasses.
Abram drives them away.
The first thing that moves toward the covenant pieces is a scavenger.
The Cup is being prepared,
and already something comes to feed on what is dead.
Abram stands guard.
The man who could not protect his wife in Egypt now protects the covenant animals from birds that would consume them.
He holds the pieces until the sun goes down.
As the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell on Abram.
Terror and great darkness fell on him.
The same sleep that fell on Adam in chapter two,
when God took a rib and made the woman,
now falls on Abram.
But where Adam's sleep preceded a gift,
Abram's sleep precedes a prophecy of suffering.
And where Adam was not afraid,
Abram is surrounded by terror and great darkness.
God speaks:
Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs.
They will be slaves there.
They will be afflicted for four hundred years.
But I will bring judgment on that nation they serve.
And afterward they shall come out with great possessions.
The Cup that was promised, offspring, land, blessing,
will pass through slavery before it arrives.
The son God promised will produce a nation.
That nation will be carried into a land that is not theirs.
They will serve.
They will suffer.
For four hundred years.
The promise does not skip over the pain.
It passes through it.
You shall go to your fathers in peace.
You shall be buried at a good old age.
In the fourth generation they shall come back here,
for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete.
God tells Abram he will die before the promise is fulfilled.
The man who believed for a son will not live to see the nation.
The Cup is given to a man who will carry it to his grave and hand it to a generation that will be born in slavery.
And the reason for the delay is not Abram's failure,
it is the patience of God with the Amorites.
The iniquity of the people who live in the promised land is not yet full.
God waits for the cup of their sin to reach the lip before He pours them out.
The same God who judged the earth with flood is measuring another people.
The Cup of judgment has a timer,
and it has not yet run out.
Then the sun goes down.
It is dark.
A smoking firepot and a flaming torch pass between the pieces.
God alone.
Not Abram.
In the ancient covenant-cutting rite, both parties walked between the severed animals,
saying by their action:
may this happen to me if I break this covenant.
Both parties took the oath.
Both carried the curse.
Only God passes through.
Abram is asleep.
The man who believed is unconscious.
The covenant is cut,
and the only one who walks the corridor of blood is God Himself,
as fire and smoke, the same elements that appeared on Sinai,
the same pillar that will lead Israel through the wilderness.
God takes both sides of the oath upon Himself.
If this covenant fails, the judgment falls on God, not on Abram.
The Cup is cut unconditionally.
The promise does not depend on Abram's faithfulness.
It depends on God passing through the pieces alone.
In the dark.
As fire and smoke.
On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram:
To your offspring I give this land,
from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates.
The Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim,
the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.
Ten nations.
The land God promises is not empty.
It is full of people who have names and histories and sins that are not yet complete.
The Cup that was cut in blood is given as a deed to land that belongs to others.
The same God who scattered the nations at Babel now promises to displace ten of them,
in His own time, when their cup is full,
for the sake of a man who believed Him for a son he could not see.
The Cup is cut.
The promise is blood-sealed.
The four-hundred-year clock starts ticking.
The firepot and the torch have passed through the pieces and disappeared into the dark.
What was spoken in chapter twelve as a calling is now sealed in chapter fifteen as a covenant.
The word that came by voice is now backed by blood.
Abram stands in the dark with the pieces behind him.
He has no son.
He has no land.
He has a covenant that depends entirely on the One who walked alone through the blood.
The Cup is cut.
The vessel sleeps.
The promise holds.
